lead: Extrusion pushes a metal billet through a die opening with a hydraulic ram. The metal takes the die's cross-section and leaves as one long continuous piece. Aluminium window sections, heat-sink fins, ladder rails and toothpaste tubes are made this way. This chapter covers direct, indirect and impact extrusion, and the defects that spoil the product.
prereq: You need: 2.1 for hot and cold working and for the mean flow stress σ̄.

sections.h3: Ram, container, die: the basic setup

blocks.text: An extrusion press has three parts. The container is a thick steel cylinder. A die with the required opening is clamped at one end. A ram enters at the other end and pushes a billet, a solid metal cylinder, often preheated. The metal upsets, flows through the die and leaves as a continuous length: a 300 mm billet becomes many metres of bar. Rolling and forging shape metal in steps or blows (see 2.2 and 2.3); extrusion makes one constant cross-section in a single push.
The taper leading into the die opening is the die angle, quoted as the included angle 2α, where α is the semi-die angle measured from the extrusion axis.

blocks.where: R is the extrusion ratio (no unit); A₀ is the billet cross-section area in mm²; A_f is the product cross-section area in mm²; D₀ is the billet diameter in mm and D_f the product diameter in mm, for round sections only.

blocks.text: R measures how hard the pass is. Cold extrusion keeps R below about 3 for steel, because flow stress is already high. Hot extrusion of aluminium runs at R from about 10 to 100, and thin hollow sections need the upper end.

blocks.where: p is the ideal extrusion pressure in MPa (1 MPa = 1 N/mm²); σ̄ is the mean flow stress of the metal in MPa; ln R is the natural logarithm of the extrusion ratio.

blocks.text: This p pays only for changing the shape. Real ram pressure is higher, because friction on the container wall and internal shearing add to it (see 2.6).

sections.h3: Direct and indirect: where the friction sits

blocks.text: Direct (forward) extrusion is the common picture. The ram touches the billet and pushes it down the container; the die stays at the far end. The billet slides against the container wall over its whole length, so friction is large. Ram pressure is highest just after flow starts, falls as the billet shortens and less of it rubs, and rises slightly at the end when the short butt is squeezed out. That butt is left behind and cut off.

Indirect (backward) extrusion moves the die instead. The die sits on the front of a hollow ram and the far end of the container is closed by a solid block. The ram pushes the die into the billet; metal flows backwards through the die and up the hollow bore. The billet does not slide on the container wall, so that friction disappears. Ram force is lower for the same reduction, often by a quarter or more, and a larger R per pass becomes possible.

The price is mechanical. A hollow ram is weaker, so press capacity limits the work, and the product must pass through the ram. Die friction remains in both arrangements: the die surface still rubs on the flowing metal.

Impact extrusion is a single-blow cold process. A slug of soft metal sits in a die cavity. A punch comes down fast, and the metal has nowhere to go but up through the narrow gap between punch and die wall, so a thin-walled cup with a closed bottom forms in a fraction of a second. Toothpaste tubes, aerosol cans and zinc battery cases are made this way. The metal flows instead of being squeezed flat, so the wall can be far thinner than the punch travel.

Hydrostatic extrusion surrounds the billet with a fluid, oil or a polymer, at high pressure. The fluid itself drives the billet through the die. No ram touches the billet and there is no container friction. The whole billet is under compression, so brittle metals can be extruded, and two metals can be clad in one pass. Sealing the high-pressure fluid makes the equipment costly.

sections.h3: Hot or cold, tubes, and what goes wrong

blocks.text: Hot extrusion runs above the recrystallisation temperature (see 2.1). Flow stress is low, so R can be large and the press smaller, but oxide scale spoils the surface; steel is usually extruded with a glass lubricant that melts into a protective film. Cold extrusion runs at room temperature, needs phosphate coating and soap lubricant, and gives a smooth, accurate, strain-hardened product at higher flow stress and a smaller R per pass.

With a flat-faced die, metal in the corners stops moving and forms a dead-metal zone. It acts like a natural die of smaller angle and makes flow more uniform, but lumps of it can break away into the product. Die angle is a compromise: too small and the die surface is long and rubs; too large and the metal shears internally.

For a tube, metal flows through an annular gap between the die and a mandrel, a fixed or floating plug that sets the bore. A port-hole die splits the billet into legs around a central mandrel, and the legs weld back together under pressure, giving hollow aluminium profiles such as window frames and heat sinks.

items: Pipe (tailpipe): at the back end the flow turns inward and drags surface oxide and lubricant to the axis, leaving a hollow pipe. Discard the butt.
Surface cracking, bambooing: transverse cracks in rings like a bamboo stem, from hot shortness, too high a temperature or too fast a ram.
Chevron cracking (centre burst): arrow-shaped cracks on the axis, from tensile stress in the core when R is low or the die angle large.
Die lines and blistering: longitudinal marks from a worn die; blisters from gas or lubricant trapped under the skin.

blocks.text: The machine is a horizontal hydraulic press, so the long product runs out along the floor. Aluminium window sections, heat sinks, ladder rails, door frames and copper busbars are typical products.

figure.caption: The four extrusion routes and how the ram or fluid acts in each. Notice that only the indirect route removes sliding between billet and container wall; impact is a cold single-blow variant.

spec.aria: A classification tree of extrusion into direct, indirect, impact and hydrostatic, each with a short note on how the ram or fluid acts.

examples.question: A 100 mm diameter aluminium billet is direct extruded into a 40 mm diameter bar. The mean flow stress of the aluminium at the working temperature is 200 MPa. Find the extrusion ratio, the ideal extrusion pressure, the ram force and the percentage area reduction.
steps: Billet area A₀ = (π/4) × 100² = 7854 mm². Product area A_f = (π/4) × 40² = 1257 mm².
Extrusion ratio R = 7854 / 1257 = 6.25, or directly (100/40)² = 6.25. It is an area ratio, so the diameter ratio is squared.
Ideal pressure p = σ̄ ln R = 200 × ln 6.25 = 200 × 1.8326 = 366.5 MPa.
Area reduction = 1 − A_f / A₀ = 1 − 1/6.25 = 0.84, that is 84%.
The real press load is above 2.88 MN: container friction and internal shearing add to the ideal pressure, so a press of roughly 3.5 to 4 MN is selected.
examples.answer: R = 6.25, ideal pressure = 366.5 MPa, ram force = 2.88 MN, and the area reduction is 84%.
examples.check:
import math

d0 = 100.0     # billet diameter, mm
df = 40.0      # product diameter, mm
sigma = 200.0  # mean flow stress, MPa = N/mm^2

R = (d0 / df) ** 2
p = sigma * math.log(R)
A0 = math.pi / 4 * d0 ** 2
F = p * A0 / 1e6          # newtons -> meganewtons
red = (1 - 1 / R) * 100   # percent

print(R)
print(round(p, 1))
print(round(A0))
print(round(F, 2))
print(round(red, 1))

traps: R is an area ratio. Writing R = 100/40 = 2.5 instead of (100/40)² = 6.25 throws the whole calculation off.
Indirect extrusion removes billet–container friction, not die friction. The die still rubs on the flowing metal in every route.
p = σ̄ ln R is the ideal pressure. Treating it as the press load ignores friction and redundant work, which add 30 to 60%.

Pipe and chevron cracking are different defects. Pipe is a hollow channel at the back end on the axis, fed by surface oxide; chevron cracks are internal arrowheads in the core, driven by tensile stress.
1 MPa = 1 N/mm². Multiply pressure in MPa by area in mm² to get newtons; mixing millimetres with metres gives an error of 10⁶.

quiz.q: Define extrusion ratio and state the units of the quantities in it.
quiz.a: R = A₀/A_f, the billet cross-section area divided by the product cross-section area. Both areas are in mm², so R has no unit.

quiz.q: Why does the ram pressure in direct extrusion fall as the billet gets shorter, even though the metal is strain hardening?
quiz.a: Friction depends on the contact length with the container wall. As the billet shortens, less area rubs, and the friction term drops faster than strain hardening raises the flow stress.

quiz.q: Indirect extrusion needs a lower force. Why then is direct extrusion still widely used?
quiz.a: The hollow ram of the indirect press is weaker, so force capacity and billet size are limited, and the product must pass through the ram. The direct press is simpler and stronger.

quiz.q: An 80 mm diameter billet is extruded to a 25 mm diameter bar with a mean flow stress of 150 MPa. Find the extrusion ratio and the ideal extrusion pressure.
Explain why impact extrusion can make a toothpaste tube wall much thinner than the punch stroke.
quiz.a: The slug is trapped in the die, so the punch displaces a fixed volume of metal. The metal flows up the narrow annular gap, and volume conservation forces a long thin wall. Wall thickness is set by the gap, not by punch travel.

quiz.q: Chevron cracks appear along the centre line of a directly extruded bar. Explain the stress state behind them and suggest two changes to reduce them.
quiz.a: The die converges and the surface material slows, so the core is pulled ahead and develops longitudinal tension; the hydrostatic pressure in the core falls and voids open into arrowhead cracks. Reduce by raising R, using a smaller die angle, or lowering ram speed and friction by better lubrication.

quiz.q: A batch of extruded aluminium shows transverse cracks like a bamboo stem. Name the defect, state one likely cause and name one defect it can be confused with.
quiz.a: Bambooing, that is surface cracking from hot shortness — temperature too high, or ram speed too high for the alloy. It can be confused with die lines, but die lines are continuous longitudinal scratches, while bambooing cracks run across the axis.

beyond: Not for the exam. On a shop floor, extrusion is judged by how long the die survives and how straight the product comes out, so die bearings and run-out tables matter as much as press tonnage. Aluminium extrusion is a large Indian industry serving construction, transport and electronics cooling.
